prompt: Write a full PRD for a new saved-search feature in our SaaS product.
assertions: States scope explicitly as in/out/future, not just a feature description
Acceptance criteria are written as Given/When/Then across happy, edge, error, and non-functional cases
Distinguishes facts, inferences, and assumptions rather than asserting all claims as fact
Names the target segment and the objective the feature serves
Lists open questions with an owner rather than leaving them implicit

prompt: Size the TAM/SAM/SOM for our AI code-review tool in the US mid-market segment.
assertions: TAM/SAM/SOM are each presented as a range, never a single point estimate
Each figure carries a source-calibrated confidence tier
At least two sizing methods are used (e.g. top-down and bottom-up), or the single-method limitation is stated explicitly
TAM is not used as a stand-in for achievable revenue — revenue projections derive from SOM
Named sources or an explicit 'no source available' statement backs every figure

prompt: Rank these 10 backlog candidates and give us a roadmap.
assertions: More than one applicable prioritization framework is actually run against the candidate list, not just one
An agreement/divergence comparison across frameworks is reported as a finding, not collapsed into a single ranked list
Where frameworks disagree, the named driver behind the divergence is stated for each divergent item
Missing inputs are flagged rather than silently fabricated to force a score
Produces a Now/Next/Later outcome roadmap, not just a raw score table

prompt: Write the PRD for our AI agent that auto-drafts customer support replies before a human sends them.
assertions: An eval set is defined and registered as the PRD's acceptance criteria, not left as a separate implementation detail
Capability and failure modes are mapped per job the agent performs
A human-in-the-loop autonomy decision (e.g. draft-only vs auto-send) with an escalation path is stated
Non-determinism, latency, cost, and safety are named as product risks, not omitted
States the model-choice hypothesis and its rationale

prompt: Define our North Star metric and a full metric tree for the product.
assertions: A single North Star metric is named, not a bundle of equally-weighted metrics
The tree decomposes into input, health, and counter-metrics across the stated four layers
Every optimized metric is paired with a counter-metric guardrail
The North Star and any OKRs are stated as a number, a %, or a named segment — never an unquantified superlative

prompt: Help us validate whether checkout abandonment is a real problem before we design a fix.
assertions: Every claim is tagged Fact, Inference, or Assumption rather than presented uniformly as truth
Assumptions are routed to the risk register rather than fabricated into a fact
Produces a validated-problem statement and an Opportunity Solution Tree, not a jump straight to a solution
States what evidence exists versus what remains to be gathered
